title: Enums and flags
body: An enum gives names to a set of integral constants: `enum Status { Pending, Active, Closed }`. By default the underlying type is `int` and members count up from 0. Enums make code self-documenting and let the compiler reject passing an arbitrary string where a status is expected.

An enum value is just its underlying number, so any int can be cast to the enum even if no member has that value: `(Status)42` is legal. Validate input with `Enum.IsDefined` or `Enum.TryParse(text, ignoreCase: true, out Status s)` and handle unknown values in switches with a default arm.

`ToString()` returns the member name, which is convenient for logging but couples output to identifiers; renaming a member changes the text. `Enum.GetValues<Status>()` enumerates the members in numeric order.

A `[Flags]` enum uses powers of two so members can be combined with `|`: `Permissions.Read | Permissions.Write`. Test a flag with `(value & Permissions.Write) != 0` or `HasFlag`. Include a `None = 0` member and never use 0 for a real flag, because `x & 0` is always 0.

When adding a member later, check every switch over the enum; the compiler only warns about missing cases in switch expressions without a discard arm. Treat enums read from files or networks as untrusted numbers until validated.

challenge: Define [Flags] enum Days with Monday..Sunday as powers of two, plus Weekend = Saturday | Sunday. Print whether Weekend includes Sunday and print Weekend itself.
question: Is `(Status)42` legal when Status has only members 0, 1 and 2?
correct: Yes; enums accept any value of the underlying type
wrong: No; it is a compile-time error
reasoning: Enums are named integers. Validate with Enum.IsDefined or TryParse and keep a default arm in switches.
